case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an order denying a federal contractor’s derivative sovereign immunity defense at summary judgment is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine rather than reviewable only after final judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (appellate jurisdiction over “final decisions” of district courts) and the judicially created collateral-order doctrine (as an exception to finality).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor acts as the government’s agent and follows government directions, so the right would be irretrievably lost if the contractor must proceed through discovery and trial before obtaining appellate review; therefore, a denial of that immunity should qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine, akin to immediate appeals permitted for qualified immunity and certain sovereign or governmental immunities.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Menocal and the other respondents argue that so-called derivative sovereign immunity for contractors is not a true immunity from suit in the way sovereign immunity or qualified immunity is, but at most a defense tied to the merits (e.g., whether the contractor exceeded authority or acted negligently), making it unsuitable for collateral-order review; permitting interlocutory appeals would expand the narrow collateral-order doctrine, increase delay and piecemeal appeals in contractor cases, and § 1291’s final-judgment rule should control with review available after final judgment.
key_precedents: CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari, 141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (cert proceedings referenced as involving the same interlocutory-appeal question)
Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940) (foundation for contractor derivative sovereign immunity when acting pursuant to valid federal authority)
The collateral-order doctrine line of cases under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (e.g., Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541 (1949))
Combs, 52 S.W.2d 720 (state case cited in the amici discussion for the idea that a contractor acting as a government agent may share the government’s immunity when acting non-negligently)
Nelson (Minnesota Supreme Court blasting/bridge-construction case referenced for treating contractor as an “agent of the state” and linking contractor liability to the state’s)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Respondent because §1291’s final-judgment rule is a threshold constraint, and petitioner’s best analogy—Yearsley as an immunity from suit—does not satisfy Cohen’s strict, element-by-element requirements. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the authority-and-compliance questions that define Yearsley are typically intertwined with the merits and often factbound at the summary-judgment stage, defeating the “completely separate” prong. And even if the litigation burdens are substantial, Mohawk teaches that ordinary burdens do not render an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment; an erroneous denial can be corrected on appeal then. I would therefore assign a narrow opinion holding only that a summary-judgment denial of Yearsley in the presence of genuine factual disputes is not immediately appealable, leaving open any different case presenting a purely legal Yearsley question.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is an immunity from suit and thus should be immediately appealable lest the right be lost through trial. But §1291 authorizes appeals only from “final decisions,” and I share Chief Justice Roberts’s insistence that any collateral-order carveout remain truly narrow rather than expanded by functional analogy. As Justice Alito explains, Yearsley denials commonly turn on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and complied with federal directions—merits-adjacent, often factbound questions that fail Cohen’s “completely separate from the merits” requirement and remain correctable on appeal after final judgment. Whatever the litigation burdens, Mohawk’s restraint counsels against judicially creating a new interlocutory-appeal category in an area Congress can address by statute or rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley should be treated as an immunity from suit, and thus that the right is effectively lost if the contractor must endure trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Yearsley questions—valid federal authorization and compliance with federal directions—are typically intertwined with the merits and frequently fact-bound at the summary-judgment stage, so the denial does not satisfy Cohen’s requirement of separateness. And under Mohawk, the ordinary burdens of litigation do not make an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment; post-judgment review can still correct an erroneous rejection of the defense without expanding a narrow, judge-made exception to § 1291. Recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would predictably generate piecemeal appeals across routine contractor cases, undermining the administrable final-judgment rule Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best contention—that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose value is lost if the contractor must endure discovery and trial—does not satisfy Cohen’s stringent requirements. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Yearsley inquiry here turns on authority-and-compliance questions intertwined with the merits and often dependent on disputed facts, so it is not “completely separate from the merits.” And as Justice Barrett notes, once the case proceeds, the trial record will supersede the summary-judgment record, reinforcing why post-judgment review remains meaningful; ordinary litigation burdens are not enough to expand the “small class” of collateral orders absent congressional authorization. Recognizing immediate appealability would also risk forcing protective, piecemeal appeals in a broad run of contractor cases, contrary to basic finality principles under §1291.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is the analogy to qualified immunity: if Yearsley is truly an immunity from suit, then the right is effectively lost absent immediate appeal. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, the Yearsley inquiry here—validly conferred federal authority and compliance with federal directions—is bound up with the merits and disputed facts, so it flunks Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement and looks far more like an ordinary defense than a categorical structural immunity. And under Mohawk, litigation burden alone does not justify expanding the “small class” of collateral orders; post-judgment review can still vindicate an erroneously rejected Yearsley defense. I do not see a vehicle here to create a new interlocutory-appeal category absent congressional authorization, and a fact-bound summary-judgment denial is the weakest posture for doing so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest submission—that Yearsley is styled as an immunity from suit and so must be immediately appealable—cannot carry the day under §1291 and Cohen’s narrow, judge-made exception. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the authority-and-compliance questions central to Yearsley are commonly merits-adjacent and factbound, so the denial is not “completely separate from the merits,” and that alone defeats collateral-order jurisdiction. And Justice Barrett is right to stress that post-judgment review remains meaningful: the claimed harm is largely the ordinary burdens of litigation, which Mohawk instructs us is not a sufficient basis for enlarging this “small class” of collateral orders. If contractor cases warrant a new interlocutory-appeal path, Congress (or the rules process) is the proper source for it, not our further expansion of Cohen.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest petitioner point is that Yearsley functions like an immunity from suit, so denial should be immediately appealable under Cohen because the right is effectively lost if the contractor must stand trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Yearsley inquiry—valid federal authorization and compliance with federal directions—typically overlaps with the merits and is often factbound at summary judgment, which means it is not “completely separate” in the way Cohen requires. And under Mohawk and related cases, ordinary litigation burdens are not enough to expand §1291’s narrow collateral-order exception where post-judgment review can still vindicate the defense. Recognizing interlocutory jurisdiction here would create a broad, administratively unworkable new category of piecemeal appeals in contractor cases, contrary to the final-judgment rule Congress enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention—that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose value is irretrievably lost absent immediate appeal—does not satisfy Cohen’s stringent prerequisites. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan both emphasize, the authority-and-compliance inquiry typically overlaps with the merits and is often factbound at summary judgment, so it is not “completely separate,” and interlocutory review would invite routine piecemeal appeals in contractor litigation. And under Ortiz, if the case proceeds to trial, the trial record supersedes the summary-judgment record, underscoring why post-judgment review remains meaningful rather than “effectively unreviewable.” Whatever the burdens of litigation, Mohawk’s insistence on a “small class” of collateral orders counsels against creating a new appeal category absent a categorical immunity whose core protection is the avoidance of trial itself.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s best contention is that Yearsley functions as an immunity from suit whose value is irretrievably lost absent immediate appeal, akin to qualified immunity. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the asserted Yearsley protection here depends on authority-and-compliance determinations that substantially overlap with the merits and are often factbound at the summary-judgment stage, so the denial is not “completely separate from the merits” under Cohen. And consistent with Justice Barrett’s point, post-judgment review remains available to vindicate the defense; litigation burdens alone cannot justify enlarging §1291’s narrow collateral-order category. Recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction for routine Yearsley denials would invite piecemeal appeals and improperly expand interlocutory review without clear congressional authorization.

John Roberts.reasoning: Our first obligation under § 1291 is to confirm appellate jurisdiction, and the collateral-order doctrine remains a “narrow” exception that we apply element by element. Although a denial of Yearsley derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment may be conclusive for the moment, the asserted protection is not “conceptually distinct from the merits” here: it turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and adhered to the Government’s directions—issues that substantially overlap with liability facts. Nor is the order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment in the way sovereign or qualified immunity is, because the contractor’s claim largely functions as a defense to liability rather than a categorical entitlement not to stand trial, and ordinary litigation burdens alone do not justify expanding collateral-order review. Allowing immediate appeal would risk transforming routine merits disputes in contractor cases into piecemeal interlocutory appeals, contrary to § 1291’s final-judgment rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291’s text limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a judicially created exception that should remain narrow rather than expanded to new categories not grounded in the statute’s original public meaning. A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim for contractors typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and complied with the Government’s directions—questions intertwined with the merits and often dependent on factbound disputes, making the denial at summary judgment ill-suited for immediate appeal. Unlike true immunities from suit rooted in constitutional structure (e.g., sovereign or Eleventh Amendment immunity), this contractor defense can be vindicated after final judgment through an ordinary appeal, even if that entails litigation burdens. Allowing interlocutory review here would invite piecemeal appeals in routine contractor cases and further untether the collateral-order doctrine from §1291’s final-judgment rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1291 authorizes appeals only from “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judicially created exception that we have repeatedly refused to expand simply because a litigant asserts a “right not to stand trial.” A denial of Yearsley-based derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically turns on whether the contractor in fact acted within valid federal authority and complied with governmental directions—questions intertwined with the merits—so it fails Cohen’s requirement that the issue be “completely separate from the merits.” And whatever protection the contractor claims can be vindicated after final judgment (or through available procedural mechanisms), whereas recognizing an immediate appeal here would invite piecemeal appeals in a broad class of contractor cases, contrary to § 1291’s finality rule. In keeping with our admonition that the collateral-order doctrine remain “stringent” and of “modest scope,” I would hold the order not immediately appealable.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the basic principle that appellate review ordinarily awaits final judgment, and the collateral-order doctrine remains a “narrow” exception that we have repeatedly refused to expand absent a right that is clearly and categorically lost if trial proceeds. A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim at summary judgment typically turns on merits-bound questions—whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and followed the Government’s directions—so the denial is not sufficiently “separate from the merits” to qualify as a collateral order under settled precedent. Treating such denials as immediately appealable would invite piecemeal, protective interlocutory appeals in a broad swath of contractor litigation, departing from centuries of finality principles and our caution in cases like Mohawk and Will. Any further expansion of interlocutory review in this area is for Congress, not a judicial enlargement of Cohen.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Sticking to the question presented—collateral-order appealability under §1291—this denial of a contractor’s Yearsley/derivative-immunity defense does not fit the narrow class of immediately appealable immunity orders. Unlike Eleventh Amendment or qualified immunity (where we have treated the entitlement as a true immunity from suit that is “effectively lost” absent immediate review, Puerto Rico Aqueduct), a Yearsley defense typically turns on fact-bound merits-adjacent questions—whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority and followed federal directions—making it poorly suited to collateral-order treatment and adequately reviewable after final judgment. Extending collateral-order jurisdiction here would infer major interlocutory-appeal consequences from analogy and structure rather than from the settled, carefully cabined immunity categories our cases recognize, inviting precisely the piecemeal review §1291 is meant to prevent. On this record and posture (summary-judgment denial with authority/compliance disputes), the asserted right is not sufficiently separate from the merits nor irretrievably lost to justify immediate appeal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 makes finality the rule, and recognizing an immediate appeal here would require extending Cohen’s collateral-order doctrine to a new contractor-immunity category—something this Court has repeatedly instructed must remain “narrow and selective.” A denial of Yearsley/derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically turns on fact-bound questions about the contractor’s authority and conduct (e.g., whether it exceeded government directions), so the issue is not “completely separate from the merits” in the way true immunities are. Nor is the ruling “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, because any error in rejecting the defense can be remedied on ordinary appeal without judicially enlarging interlocutory jurisdiction where Congress has not clearly authorized it. Institutional restraint counsels leaving any broader interlocutory-review regime for contractor defenses to Congress or the rulemaking process, not judicial expansion of Cohen.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: So the narrow question is whether a denial at summary judgment of a federal contractor’s Yearsley/derivative-sovereign-immunity defense qualifies as a “final decision” under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 via the collateral-order doctrine. Under this Court’s stringent collateral-order cases, the relevant “class of claims” (Yearsley denials) typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and followed government directions—issues that are intertwined with the merits and often depend on disputed facts, so the order does not “resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits.” And even if the contractor must proceed to discovery and trial, the asserted protection is not a traditionally recognized immunity from suit of the kind this Court has treated as “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment (as with qualified immunity), but rather a liability-limiting defense reviewable on appeal from a final judgment. Given § 1291’s final-judgment rule and this Court’s repeated refusal to expand the “small class” of collateral orders, the denial here is not immediately appealable.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291 makes interlocutory review the exception, and the collateral-order doctrine remains “narrow and selective,” so the question is whether this summary-judgment order is effectively final because the asserted right would be irretrievably lost if review waited until final judgment. A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” defense typically turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority and complied with federal directions—fact-bound questions that are intertwined with the merits and often depend on a fuller record, meaning trial and later proceedings can supersede the summary-judgment record in the way Ortiz explains, with meaningful review still available after final judgment. Unlike qualified immunity or Eleventh Amendment immunity, this contractor defense is not a paradigmatic entitlement to avoid trial itself as a categorical matter; treating it as immediately appealable would expand collateral-order review beyond the limited classes this Court has recognized. Because post-judgment review remains practicable and the issue is not sufficiently separate from the merits, I would hold the denial not immediately appealable.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under §1291’s final-judgment rule, the collateral-order doctrine remains a “narrow and selective” exception, and GEO must show the denial of its Yearsley-based derivative immunity is conclusively resolved, wholly separate from the merits, and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Here, the contractor’s asserted protection turns on fact- and merits-bound questions—whether GEO acted within valid federal authority and followed Government directions (or instead exceeded authority or acted wrongfully)—so the summary-judgment denial is not “completely separate from the merits” in the way true immunity-from-suit rulings (e.g., qualified immunity) can be. And whatever cost of litigation GEO identifies is not the kind of irreparable consequence that justifies expanding collateral-order review, because the defense can be vindicated on appeal after final judgment without creating a new, freestanding right to avoid trial. Treating Yearsley as automatically conferring an immediately appealable immunity would improperly broaden the collateral-order doctrine beyond its modest scope and invite the very piecemeal appeals §1291 is designed to prevent.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an order denying a federal contractor’s claim of “derivative sovereign immunity” at summary judgment is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-judgment rule), as interpreted through the judicially created collateral-order doctrine (Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when the contractor acted as the government’s agent within the scope of federal direction/authorization; therefore, a denial of that protection is effectively unreviewable after final judgment because the contractor will have already borne the very burdens (discovery, trial, and litigation costs) immunity is meant to prevent. GEO and supporting amici contend immediate appellate review is needed to prevent disruption to federal contracting, avoid chilling contractors from performing sensitive governmental functions, and align derivative sovereign immunity with other immunities that receive collateral-order appeals (e.g., qualified immunity).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Menocal and supporting amici (and the United States as amicus supporting respondents on the jurisdictional question) argue that a denial of derivative sovereign immunity is not the type of narrow, categorical immunity-from-suit determination that qualifies for collateral-order review. They contend the defense is commonly fact-bound (turning on contract scope, governmental direction, and compliance), can be adequately reviewed after final judgment, and allowing interlocutory appeals would expand the collateral-order doctrine beyond its strict limits—inviting delay and piecemeal appeals in ordinary civil litigation involving contractors.
key_precedents: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (collateral-order doctrine framework)
CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari (cert-stage history noted; Court invited SG views on same collateral-order issue)
Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. (foundation for contractor derivative sovereign immunity, often described as immunity when acting under valid federal authority)
Combs (Ky. case cited in amici discussion of contractors as state agents with immunity when non-negligent)
Nelson (Minn. case cited for contractor as "agent of the state" and liability tied to the state’s)

John Roberts.reasoning: We must satisfy ourselves of §1291 jurisdiction before any merits inquiry, and the denial here does not fit Cohen’s narrow collateral-order class. The strongest petitioner argument—that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose benefits are lost absent immediate review—fails because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the Yearsley determination in this posture turns on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance, which are intertwined with the merits and are not categorically conclusive or “completely separate.” And as Justice Alito notes, the asserted harm is largely the ordinary burden of litigation, which Mohawk and Digital Equipment hold is not enough to expand collateral-order review, particularly where errors can be corrected after final judgment. Recognizing jurisdiction here would invite routine piecemeal appeals in contractor disputes and erode §1291’s final-judgment rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that Yearsley operates as an immunity from suit, so its value is lost absent immediate appeal. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain, the Yearsley inquiry in this posture is typically fact-bound—turning on the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance—so it is neither “conclusive” nor “completely separate from the merits” in Cohen’s categorical sense. Unlike the States’ structural sovereign immunity (which reflects a constitutional allocation of authority and fiscal accountability, and thus warrants special solicitude), this contractor protection is conditional and applied through accreted, judge-made doctrine with indistinct boundaries, making it a poor candidate for further collateral-order expansion. Any error can be remedied after final judgment without rewriting §1291 to accommodate routine contractor disputes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is the Puerto Rico Aqueduct analogy—that Yearsley supplies an immunity from suit whose denial should be immediately appealable—but that analogy depends on a right that is both categorically separable from the merits and effectively lost if review awaits final judgment. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Yearsley in this posture turns on contract scope, federal authorization, and compliance—fact-bound, merits-entangled questions that are not “completely separate” or reliably “conclusive” under Cohen when assessed categorically, and thus are a poor vehicle for collateral-order expansion. And, as Justice Kagan notes, what is chiefly claimed to be lost here is the ordinary burden of litigation, which Mohawk and Digital Equipment tell us is not enough to create interlocutory appellate jurisdiction. Given §1291’s final-judgment rule and our repeated insistence that Cohen remain narrow and administrable, I would dismiss for lack of jurisdiction without reaching broader characterizations of Yearsley.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention is that Yearsley is an immunity from suit, so its denial should be immediately appealable under Puerto Rico Aqueduct. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, the Yearsley inquiry in this posture turns on fact-bound, merits-linked questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance, which makes the denial neither categorically “conclusive” nor “completely separate” under Cohen as constrained by Mohawk and Digital Equipment. And even accepting the “immunity” label, what is lost absent interlocutory review is largely the ordinary burden of litigation, not the kind of structural sovereign prerogative that renders an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment. Expanding collateral-order jurisdiction here would predictably invite piecemeal appeals in routine contractor disputes, undermining §1291’s final-judgment rule.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is the Puerto Rico Aqueduct analogy: if Yearsley is an immunity from suit, its value is lost once the case proceeds. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, this summary-judgment denial turns on scope-of-authorization and compliance questions that are fact-laden and intertwined with the merits, so it fails Cohen’s separateness and conclusiveness requirements when assessed categorically. Accepting petitioner’s framing would effectively treat any contractor’s conditional, compliance-dependent defense as immediately appealable, collapsing Cohen’s factors and inviting the piecemeal appellate regime Mohawk and Digital Equipment reject. Postjudgment review remains adequate here because what is chiefly at stake is avoiding ordinary litigation burdens, not a structural sovereign prerogative that our cases have deemed effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is styled as an immunity from suit, and under Puerto Rico Aqueduct the denial of certain immunities can be immediately appealable because the right is lost if litigation proceeds. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan underscore, the Yearsley inquiry in this posture is typically conditional and fact-bound—turning on the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance—so it is not categorically “conclusive” or “completely separate from the merits” as Cohen and Mohawk demand. And as Justice Alito warns, recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would create a new, expansive class of piecemeal appeals in ordinary contractor litigation, exactly the sort of doctrinal accretion §1291 and our precedents counsel against. Whatever interest remains can be vindicated on appeal after final judgment, and the ordinary burdens of litigation do not satisfy the stringent “effectively unreviewable” requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument is that Yearsley operates as an immunity-from-suit and therefore denial should be immediately appealable under Mitchell and Puerto Rico Aqueduct. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the Yearsley inquiry at summary judgment typically turns on fact-bound, merits-intertwined questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance, which makes the order neither categorically “conclusive” nor “completely separate from the merits” under Cohen as narrowed by Digital Equipment and Mohawk. And even if the contractor has a substantial interest in avoiding litigation, Mohawk’s framework treats ordinary litigation burdens as insufficient to render the order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, especially where the asserted protection is conditional rather than structural. Recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would predictably expand interlocutory review to routine contractor disputes, contrary to §1291’s final-judgment rule and our repeated insistence that Cohen remain narrow.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is styled as an immunity from suit, so the denial should be immediately appealable under Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Mitchell. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the Yearsley determination at summary judgment typically turns on scope-of-authorization and compliance questions that are intertwined with the merits and often fact-dependent, so it is not “completely separate” or reliably “conclusive” in Cohen’s categorical sense. That makes it closer to the class of interlocutory rulings §1291 requires us to defer—and, consistent with Ortiz’s record-supersession logic, the interlocutory record is a poor vehicle for final resolution of sufficiency-bound disputes that trial may reshape. Any error remains reviewable after final judgment, and recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would broaden Cohen into an administratively unstable category of routine contractor appeals contrary to Mohawk and Digital Equipment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention is that Yearsley operates as an immunity from suit, and thus the denial should be immediately appealable under Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Mitchell because the asserted entitlement would be lost if litigation proceeds. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Yearsley determination in this posture is commonly fact-bound—turning on the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with federal direction—so it is not categorically “completely separate from the merits” or reliably “conclusive” in Cohen’s narrow class. Under Mohawk and Digital Equipment, the ordinary burdens of litigation do not make an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, and postjudgment review remains available to correct any error without expanding §1291 through an administratively unstable new category of collateral-order appeals. For those reasons, I continue to conclude we lack appellate jurisdiction here.

John Roberts.reasoning: We must assure our jurisdiction before reaching any merits, and §1291 permits interlocutory review only within the narrow Cohen collateral-order class. Although a denial of true immunity from suit is often immediately appealable (as in Puerto Rico Aqueduct), Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” for contractors typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with federal direction—fact-bound questions intertwined with the merits at summary judgment rather than a conceptually distinct sovereign prerogative. The litigation burdens GEO identifies (discovery and trial costs) are generally reviewable after final judgment, and recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would invite piecemeal appeals in ordinary contractor suits beyond Cohen’s strict limits. The Court therefore lacks §1291 jurisdiction over this interlocutory appeal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Sovereign immunity is a structural protection for the government itself—guarding democratic accountability and the public fisc—and waiver is therefore a critical threshold inquiry; a federal contractor’s asserted “derivative” protection is not the same constitutional or structural immunity recognized in cases like Alden, and it should not be transformed by judge-made extension into an automatic immunity-from-suit triggering interlocutory review. Under Cohen, a denial of Yearsley/derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment is often fact-bound and intertwined with the merits because it turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and complied with federal direction, making it neither sufficiently “separate from the merits” nor reliably “conclusive.” Expanding collateral-order appealability here would invite piecemeal appeals in ordinary contractor litigation, shifting substantial resource-allocation decisions from the political branches to courts through an amorphous, nontextual doctrine that risks doctrinal scope-creep. Any error can be reviewed after final judgment without reworking § 1291’s final-judgment rule through further judicial accretion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The threshold question under §1291 is reviewability, and the collateral-order doctrine remains a “narrow” and “stringent” exception that we assess categorically rather than case-by-case. Denials of Yearsley-style derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically turn on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with governmental directions, which means the issue is not “completely separate from the merits” in the Cohen sense and is adequately reviewable after final judgment. Nor has this Court treated Yearsley as a settled, categorical “immunity from suit” comparable to the immunities we have recognized as immediately appealable; extending collateral-order review here would risk the very expansion and piecemeal appeals that Hallock, Digital Equipment, and Mohawk caution against. Because the asserted protection does not fit the small class of orders that are “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, appellate jurisdiction is lacking at this stage.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under § 1291, we permit collateral-order appeals only in the “small class” of orders that conclusively decide a question that is both wholly separate from the merits and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A denial of Yearsley-style “derivative sovereign immunity” at summary judgment typically turns on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with governmental direction—issues intertwined with the merits and not amenable to categorical, administrable interlocutory review as a class. Unlike qualified immunity or Eleventh Amendment immunity, any protection here is not a clear immunity-from-suit entitlement whose value is categorically destroyed by awaiting final judgment; postjudgment review, together with ordinary procedural gatekeeping (summary judgment and, where appropriate, certification or mandamus), suffices without expanding Cohen. Allowing immediate appeals in this contractor setting would risk turning routine disputes over contract scope and compliance into piecemeal appellate litigation, contrary to Mohawk’s insistence that the doctrine remain narrow.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The collateral-order doctrine is narrow, and GEO has not shown that a Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” denial at summary judgment fits Cohen’s second and third requirements in this case. The Yearsley inquiry here turns on contract scope, federal direction, and GEO’s compliance—questions deeply entangled with the merits and typically fact-bound—so treating the denial as “completely separate” would collapse that factor into a broad rule for contractor defenses. And because the claimed protection is conditional (not an unqualified immunity from suit like a State’s Eleventh Amendment immunity), any error can be adequately reviewed after final judgment without converting routine contractor litigation into piecemeal interlocutory appeals. Under Puerto Rico Aqueduct, immediate appeal is warranted when the defendant possesses an established right not to stand trial; this record does not present that kind of categorical, separable immunity determination.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule controls unless the contractor can bring this case within Cohen’s “narrow and selective” collateral-order exception, and doing so here would require extending that judge-made doctrine to a new class of fact-dependent summary-judgment denials. A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim typically turns on contested questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance—issues entwined with the merits and not the kind of categorical, separable immunity determination we have treated as immediately appealable. Nor is the denial “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment in the sense demanded by Mohawk and Will, because the asserted interest largely resembles avoidance of litigation burdens rather than a congressionally or historically fixed right not to be haled into court. Institutional caution counsels restraint: if federal contracting requires broader interlocutory review, Congress and the Rules Enabling Act process—not judicial expansion of Cohen—are the proper vehicles.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Start with the governing text and doctrine: §1291 embodies the final-judgment rule, and Cohen’s collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” and “stringent” exception that turns on the class of orders at issue, not the equities of a particular case. On this record, a denial of Yearsley/so-called derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically depends on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with governmental direction, which makes the issue insufficiently “completely separate from the merits” and counsels against collateral-order treatment. Nor is such an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment in the sense Digital Equipment and Mohawk require—i.e., a categorical right “not to stand trial altogether”—because Yearsley functions in many cases as a defense to liability that can be vindicated on appeal after trial rather than an across-the-board immunity-from-suit akin to qualified immunity. Given the Court’s repeated insistence that collateral-order review not expand to swallow §1291, the better reading is that immediate appeal is unavailable here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule is the baseline, and a summary-judgment denial is ordinarily an interlocutory step “along the route to final judgment,” appealable only if it fits within Cohen’s narrow collateral-order exception. A Yearsley/derivative-sovereign-immunity claim commonly turns on fact-intensive questions about the scope of federal authorization and the contractor’s compliance with federal direction, so it is not the kind of purely legal entitlement that can be decided once and for all on an interlocutory record. As Ortiz explains, once the case proceeds to trial, the full record supersedes the summary-judgment record, making immediate review of such sufficiency-bound determinations unnecessary and potentially unadministrable. Unlike Mitchell’s qualified-immunity model—where the appealable issue is a clean legal question about the right not to stand trial—this asserted protection here is adequately reviewable after final judgment without expanding Cohen beyond its strict limits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The threshold question is jurisdictional: under § 1291’s final-judgment rule, we may take this appeal only if the summary-judgment denial fits the collateral-order doctrine’s “small class,” which this Court has repeatedly kept narrow (Mohawk; Will). GEO’s Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim, as applied here, is not a categorical immunity-from-suit determination like qualified immunity; it typically turns on fact-bound questions about the contract’s scope, the Government’s authorization and direction, and the contractor’s compliance—issues entwined with the merits and readily reviewable after final judgment. Because any error can be corrected on appeal from a final judgment (with damages or a new trial remedy), the order is not “effectively unreviewable” in the Mitchell sense, and recognizing interlocutory appeal here would expand collateral-order review beyond its stringent limits. Given the United States’ position and the doctrine’s structural concern with piecemeal appeals, § 1291 does not authorize immediate review of this order.
